33 Circus Lions update

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
33 circus lions lives' changed when they were brought back to their natural environment from South America. But, it's that natural habitat that has resulted in 2 dying after ingesting a rare bacteria.

Summary:
We look at botulism (a toxin) - in a rare animal medical story - in which, two female lions died, two male lions are on the mend, from eating game meat infected with the bacteria. These circus animals were abused and treated poorly before coming to Africa - sometimes only eating chicken feet. Unlike animals in the wild who develop strong immune systems and typically survive the bacteria, these lion were never exposed to outside elements - like bacteria - before, and therefore became very ill. (Very brief description)

Further information:
We will learn about botulism and speak with Minnunette, her daughter Savannah and Jan Creamer from ADI (Who brought the animals to South Africa), and the vet who has worked very hard to save the two male lions.

SAVANNAH HEUSER

Press Release:


Circus Lions Update
The world watched in awe as 33 neglected and abused South American circus lions were rescued and released onto African soil. But just a month later, four of the cats – their immune systems compromised by years of neglect in captivity – contract a deadly bacterium that sees a veterinarian fighting to save them from certain death. Carte Blanche heads back to the Emoya Sanctuary for a bittersweet update.



Script:


In early May this year, 33 lions made a long journey from Columbia and Peru to OR Tambo international. This was the culmination of an 18 month crusade by Animal Defenders International, or ADI, to empty circus cages of their animals across South America by changing their laws.
Jan: “Everybody roared their way as they landed, announcing themselves in South Africa.”
ADI founder Jan Creamer says seeing the 33 lions encounter trees for the first time was incredibly moving.
Jan: “They literally rubbed up against the trees and the bushes, putting their front paws around the trees and just hugging them.”
Savannah Heuser inherited a farm in the Waterberg and, together with her mother Minunette, founded the Emoya Big Cat Sanctuary. It’s the ideal place to release ADI’s rescued lions who for years had known no world beyond the bars of their cages.
Savanah: “People have this fairytale image of it, bringing the lions back to Africa and I think there are a lot of factors that nobody really expected would be as serious. Lions..
Over the past month the lions have had to adapt to their first South African Winter. Rapunzel, aged 4, and Kala, 5, were soon having a ball. Savannah has a special connection with Kala – who was rescued from a circus having suffered abuse.
Savannah: “Sometimes you just look at an animal or a certain person and you click and you just think that this one was a really special one.”
Jan remembers how, at first, Kala didn’t trust humans.
Jan: “It took her a couple of weeks of love and care and making sure she realized she’d never be hurt again.”
Rapunzel and her brother lived in a circus cage the size of a double bed.
Jan: “What was so sad and heartbreaking about it was that Repunzel was afraid to come out of the cage she was in, she lived in it all her life.”
No one could have predicted what happened next.
Dr: “Saturday morning they saw that they were not getting up coming to food.”
Dr. Peter Caldwell is a wildlife veterinarian with a special interest in carnivores – especially the king of the jungle. Kala, Rapunzel and another male lion – Coco from Peru, couldn’t move.
Minunette: “You feel incredibly helpless, you don’t know how agile they’ll be if you would go in and try and help them.”
Three hours away from the farm in Pretoria North, Peter has turned this chapel into one of the worlds leading veterinary facilities. He has treated over 30 captive lions that presented with similar symptoms.
Dr: “I made a diagnosis of botulism.”
Chlostridium Botulinum is a bacterium which grows in meat or bone, however, it’s unclear when and how the lions ingested either.
Dr. “It’s not the bacteria that animals eat, it’s the toxin.”
When the bacterial spores germinate they release a strong neurotoxin. This blocks neurotransmitters released by nerve ends from being taken up by muscle cell receptors which causes temporary paralysis.
Dr: “The lions are completely awake, completely aware of what’s happening around them, but they just can’t move.”
The paralysis usually starts in the limbs and progresses throughout the body to the spine.
Dr: “The two lionesses that came in obviously had ingested a large amount of toxin. It then went to the heart muscle. I did CPR on the one lioness for 45 minutes.”
But his team lost the fight.
Dr: “That was a bad moment for us, it was very emotional for all of us.”
Sav: “I think you always take a certain responsibility for it. They were really, really lively animals, and you would think that they would remember all the bad things that happened to them, but they just forgot about it, and were really just living in the moment.”
Min: “It is also difficult for me as a mother to see how my daughter is struggling with this, and there’s no ways that I can make it better.”
While Coco was still in ICU, another male, Junior from Columbia also came down with similar symptoms. Fortunately they had ingested less of the toxin.
Dr: “Especially Coco, cos he was totally paralysed. When he started moving, there was big excitement. That lion specifically, had the fighting spirit.”
Peter has provided a feeding management programme going forward.
Dr: “This could have happened to these lions anywhere in the world it’s because these animals are what I call virgin and they are not resistant to anything in this country.”
Sav: “ We do checks several times a day, and obviously we are checking all meat supplies.”
After 2 weeks at the vet the boys get one final light sedative each - much to Juniors displeasure - to allow for their blood to be checked before their journey back home to Emoya.
Sav: “They both have siblings, you can see Coco is happy to be back with his brothers, and Junior is happy to be back with his brother.”
Back home, Junior roars to announce his return to the 30 remaining lions in the group.

PROMO 2 15 SECONDER: We watched as these kings of the jungle saw their first trees, but only a month into their African experience 4 take ill due to a rare toxin.
Dr: “The lions are completely awake, completely aware of what’s happening around them, but they just can’t move.”
PROMO 3 15 SECONDER:
Savannah: “They were both really, really lively animals.”
V/O: 4 of the 33 circus lions rescued from South America have fallen ill. Carte Blanche speaks to the team and delivers some bittersweet news.
Dr: “The lions are completely awake, but they just can’t move.”
